case.sdc.t: Cores that quietly compute wrong answers
case.sdc.what: Google and Meta found processors in their data centres that now and then gave wrong results, with no crash and no warning.
case.sdc.why: Tiny manufacturing flaws that the factory test missed, some showing up only with certain instructions, at certain temperatures, or after some ageing. Rare in one chip, but a data centre has millions of cores.
case.sdc.after: Large data centres now keep testing chips while they work, and retire the bad ones.
case.sdc.src: Meta: Detecting silent data corruptions in the wild (2022)
case.raptor.what: Owners of high-end Intel desktop processors reported crashes that began after months of use and got worse.
case.raptor.why: A clock circuit in each core aged faster under high voltage and heat, and the boards were asking for more voltage than it could take over time.
case.raptor.after: Updates capped the voltage and the warranty grew by two years. An update can stop further ageing, but it cannot undo the damage already done.
case.raptor.src: Intel: root cause of the instability (September 2024)
case.p3.what: Weeks after launch, reviewers found that Intel's fastest Pentium III crashed in some heavy jobs. Intel reproduced the problem and recalled the chip.
case.p3.why: Pushed to that speed, some chips had too little room for error in their timing. Most worked; the ones at the edge did not.
case.p3.after: A chip's speed rating must hold for the slowest chip, the hottest day and the weakest power supply, not the average. Chips are now sorted by tested speed and sold with a safety margin.
case.spectre.what: Researchers showed that almost every fast processor of the time could be tricked into leaking secrets, such as passwords, from other programs.
case.spectre.why: To run faster, processors guess ahead and do work before they know it is needed. That worked exactly as designed; nobody had imagined an attacker reading the faint traces those guesses leave behind.
case.spectre.after: Patches first, then changes in new chips. Security became a design goal next to speed, energy and cost.
case.spectre.src: Meltdown and Spectre (Graz University of Technology and others)
case.fdiv.t: The Pentium that could not divide
case.fdiv.what: A mathematics professor noticed that Intel's new Pentium sometimes gave wrong answers when dividing. The error was rare: about one in nine billion random divisions, by one estimate.
case.fdiv.why: Five entries were missing from a table inside the divider. The chip did exactly what its design said; the design was wrong, and the tests never tried those numbers.
case.fdiv.after: Intel replaced the chips. Chipmakers turned to formal verification: proving with mathematics that a circuit is right for every input, not only for the inputs someone thought to test.
case.cougar.what: Soon after launch, Intel found that a support chip for its new processors had disk ports that would wear out. New chips passed every test.
case.cougar.why: A design error put one circuit under too much stress, so it would fail after years of use. Nothing was wrong on the first day, which is why the factory test could not see it.
case.cougar.after: Intel stopped shipping, fixed the chip and replaced the old ones. Checking how every circuit ages over its whole life is now a standard step before a design goes to the factory.
case.vote.what: In a Belgian election, one candidate received more votes than were possible. A recount found 4,096 votes too many.
case.vote.why: 4,096 is exactly 2 to the power of 12: a single bit in memory had flipped from 0 to 1. A particle from space is the suspected cause, never proven.
case.vote.after: It became the classic example of a soft error, and of why memory that corrects its own errors belongs wherever a wrong number matters: servers, cars, aircraft, voting machines.
what.building.racks: Rows of tall cabinets full of computers; this is where the work is done.
what.building.cooling: Pumps and fans that carry the heat away, because every bit of electricity the chips use ends up as heat.
what.building.power: Brings in electricity from the grid and steadies it, with batteries ready if the supply drops.
what.rack.servers: Each shelf is one computer, built around a few large chips.
what.rack.switch: Connects the servers to each other and to the rest of the hall, so many machines can work as one.
what.rack.power: Turns the hall's electricity into the steady low voltage the boards need.
what.rack.cooling: Liquid flows in cold and out warm, carrying heat away from the chips.
what.board.bigchip: The chip that does the calculating: thousands of small units working at once.
what.board.memory: Holds the numbers the chip is working on, as close to it as possible.
what.board.power: Turns the board's supply into the very low, very steady voltage the chip needs.
what.board.traces: Copper lines that carry data between the memory and the chip.
what.board.connectors: Where the board plugs into the server, for power and for data.
what.chip.cores: Blocks that do the work: each fetches instructions and numbers, calculates, and passes results on.
what.chip.cache: Fast memory on the chip itself, so the cores rarely wait for the slower memory outside.
what.chip.io: The chip's doors: circuits that send and receive signals to and from everything around it.
what.chip.clock: Wires carrying the tick that keeps every part of the chip in step.
what.phone.board: The main board: the phone's chip, memory, radio and power chips, packed together.
what.phone.battery: Stores the energy for the whole day; how slowly the chip spends it decides how long it lasts.
what.phone.camera: Lenses and light sensors; much of a photo is then computed by the chip.
what.phone.antenna: Parts of the frame act as antennas, sending and receiving radio waves.
what.phoneboard.soc: The phone's chip, with its memory stacked on top of it.
what.phoneboard.pmic: The power chip: hands out the battery's energy, a different voltage to each part.
what.phoneboard.modem: Turns data into radio signals and back, following the rules every network shares.
what.phoneboard.storage: Keeps your photos, apps and messages when the power is off.
what.phone.screen: Glass over a panel of tiny lights, and a layer that feels your finger. Lit, it spends more of the battery than anything else.
what.phone.cable: Brings energy from the wall back into the battery, most often overnight.
what.phoneboard.shield: A thin metal can over the chips: it keeps their electrical noise in and the radio's signals out.
what.phoneboard.dram: The working memory sits in its own package right on top of the phone's chip: the shortest way between them, in the least space.
what.soc.cpu: General cores: big ones for heavy work, small ones that sip energy for light work.
what.soc.gpu: Many small, identical cores that draw images, all at once.
what.soc.npu: Built for the multiplications AI needs: many at a time, using little energy.
what.soc.isp: Turns the camera sensor's raw signal into a picture: colour, sharpness, noise.
what.soc.cache: Memory every district shares, so they can pass work to each other quickly.
what.car.controllers: Small computers, each in charge of one job: brakes, engine, windows, lights.
what.car.wiring: Cables that carry power and messages between the control units.
what.car.sensors: Cameras and radar that watch the road and feed the computers.
what.car.wheels: What the computers finally move: through brakes, steering and motors.
what.ecu.mcu: The small chip that makes the decisions, running one program over and over.
what.ecu.connector: Where the unit plugs into the car's wiring, for power, sensors and messages.
what.ecu.drivers: Large switches that turn real current on and off, on the small chip's command.
what.ecu.case: Metal, sealed against water, salt and shaking, with ears to bolt it to the car: it also carries the heat of the parts inside out to the car's body.
what.mcu.cores: Two small cores running the same work in step, so a mistake shows up as a difference.
what.mcu.flash: Keeps the program even when the car is switched off.
what.mcu.sram: Fast memory for the numbers the program is working on right now.
what.mcu.periph: Converts signals from sensors into numbers, talks to the car's network, keeps time.
what.crystal.sand: Quartz sand: silicon joined to oxygen, the raw material of every chip.
what.crystal.furnace: Melts purified silicon and keeps it at a steady heat for many hours.
what.crystal.melt: Molten silicon, waiting to be pulled up as a crystal.
what.crystal.ingot: A single crystal, its atoms in one unbroken pattern, pulled up slowly while it turns.
what.slice.ingot: The crystal, ready to be cut into wafers.
what.slice.saw: Fine wires running fast through the crystal, cutting many wafers at once.
what.slice.wafers: Thin discs of crystal; every chip will be built on one.
what.slice.polish: A turning pad polishes each wafer until its surface is almost perfectly flat.
what.pkg.saw: A thin, turning blade cuts the wafer apart, chip by chip.
what.pkg.substrate: The package's base: layers of wiring that spread the chip's connections out to the board.
what.pkg.bumps: Tiny drops of solder that join the chip to the package, face down.
what.pkg.die: The chip itself, flipped so its whole face can connect.
what.pkg.memory: Memory chips stacked in towers right beside the processor.
what.pkg.lid: Protects the chip and carries its heat away.
what.ship.trays: Every packaged chip is tested once more; the slower ones may be sold as a cheaper model.
what.ship.boxes: Packed and sent to the companies that build the final products.
what.ship.datacentre: Where the largest chips go: into servers in a data centre.
what.ship.phone: Where the most energy-thrifty chips go: into phones.
what.ship.car: Where the toughest chips go: into cars, for many years of heat and cold.
what.scanner.source: Makes light so short it is close to X-rays, by hitting drops of tin with a laser.
what.scanner.mirrors: Polished mirrors guide the light, because this light is swallowed by glass.
what.scanner.mask: Holds the pattern of one layer, like a stencil, magnified.
what.scanner.stage: Moves the wafer under the light with astonishing precision, exposing one chip after another.
what.scanner.vacuum: Pumps keep the inside of the machine empty of air, because this light cannot travel through air.
what.wafer.dies: The chips on this wafer, all made at once, all the same.
what.wafer.defects: Specks that landed during making; each ruins the chip it falls on.
what.die.cores: Your chip's cores, the same at every step down to here.
what.die.pads: Small metal squares where the chip connects to the outside world.
what.die.probes: Needles that touch the pads to test the chip before it is cut out.
what.die.scribe: The lane between chips, where the saw will cut.
what.block.cells: Small ready-made circuits from a library: logic gates, and flip-flops that each remember one bit. They share one height (a few span two rows), so they line up in rows.
what.block.sram: A grid of memory cells, each a small loop of switches that holds one bit while the power is on. This kind of memory is called SRAM. Its cells are drawn by hand and are not standard cells.
what.block.wires: Metal lines on many levels above the cells, connecting them.
what.gate.gates: The parts that control the switches (not logic gates). Each strip crosses both silicon strips, so one input turns one switch on and the other off.
what.gate.diff: Strips of silicon where current flows. Where a switch gate crosses a strip, the silicon under it is one switch's channel. One strip holds switches that turn on with a high gate voltage, the other switches that turn on with a low.
what.gate.metal: Wires. The two long ones bring power: one at high voltage, one at low. The other carries the result out.
what.switch.gate: The part that controls the switch (not a logic gate). It wraps around the sheets, and its voltage decides whether current can flow.
what.switch.channel: Thin sheets of silicon the current flows through.
what.switch.oxide: A very thin insulating skin that lets the gate act on the sheets without current flowing into them.
what.switch.source: Where the moving charges enter the sheets.
what.switch.drain: Where the moving charges leave the sheets.
what.atom.lattice: Silicon atoms, each joined to four neighbours in a regular pattern.
what.atom.dopant: An atom of another element, added on purpose (a dopant). It has one electron more than silicon, or one fewer, and that spare electron or gap is free to move and carry current.
what.atom.electrons: The moving charges that carry the current.
what.atom.boundary: The switch's insulating skin, seen close up. When it is only a few atoms thick, electrons can slip through.
what.clean.tool: Washes wafers one at a time with ultrapure water and chemicals, in spinning chambers behind robots.
what.deposit.tool: A sealed chamber where gases react on the hot wafer and leave a thin film.
what.deposit.gas: Bring in the gases the film is made from, in precise amounts.
what.deposit.heater: Keeps the wafer hot enough for the gases to react on its surface.
what.print.coat: Spins the wafer fast to spread a light-sensitive layer thinner than a soap bubble.
what.print.scanner: Shines light through a mask to print one layer's pattern, chip after chip across the wafer.
what.print.develop: Washes away the parts of the layer the light touched, leaving the pattern.
what.print.light: Light so short it is close to X-rays, carrying the pattern down to the wafer.
what.print.mask: Holds the pattern of one layer, like a stencil.
what.etch.tool: Fills with plasma and cuts the film where the pattern left it open.
what.etch.plasma: A glowing gas of charged particles, pulled straight down to cut straight down.
what.etch.people: Watches and tunes the machines; much of what keeps them right is know-how.
what.implant.tool: Fires a beam of atoms into the open parts of the wafer.
what.implant.beam: Atoms of another element, given a charge and sped up to strike the silicon.
what.implant.magnet: Bends the beam so that only the wanted kind of atom reaches the wafer.
what.implant.heater: Heats the wafer for a moment so the crystal heals around the new atoms.
what.wires.plating: Copper grows into the cut trenches, like plating a spoon.
what.wires.polish: A turning pad polishes the copper away until only the trenches are filled, perfectly flat.
what.wires.loop: The wafer returns to cleaning for the next layer, and the next, until all are done.
what.test.prober: Moves the wafer under a card of needles, touching one chip after another.
what.test.needles: Touch the chip's pads to send signals in and read the answers.
what.test.map: Every chip on your wafer: good ones green, the ones a speck ruined red.
what.clean.chamber: The wafer spins while a moving arm sprays it, then it is rinsed and spun dry.
what.handle.pod: A sealed box with slots for a stack of wafers. It opens only against a machine's door, so the wafers never meet the room's air.
what.handle.efem: A robot arm in a small, extra-clean room at the front of the machine. It lifts wafers out of the pod by their underside.
what.handle.lock: A small room with a door on each side. Air is pumped out before the inner door opens, so the vacuum inside the machine is never broken.
what.handle.xfer: A second robot inside the machine, carrying the wafer to whichever chamber is free. In machines that work in vacuum, it works in vacuum too.
what.handle.shelf: Where the front robot leaves the wafer for the robot inside the machine.
what.handle.dock: Where crates of pods arrive from another plant, often from another country.
what.handle.tray: After packaging, chips travel in trays, one pocket each.
handle.arrive: Docking Lowered from the track, the sealed pod lands on the machine's door. It opens only against the machine, so the wafer never meets the room's air.
handle.take: Front robot A robot arm reaches into the pod and lifts the wafer out from below, in air kept even cleaner than the room's.
handle.lock: Airlock The outer door closes behind the wafer and pumps pull the air out. Only then does the inner door open, onto the vacuum.
handle.move: Inner robot A second robot, working in the vacuum, carries the wafer to a chamber that is free.
handle.handoff: Hand-off The front robot leaves the wafer on a shelf, where a robot inside the machine picks it up.
handle.inside: Inner robot The robot inside the machine carries the wafer to a chamber that is free.
handle.back: Back the same way Robot to robot, and back into the pod. Every move is a chance to pick up a speck, so moves are few and quick.
handle.done: Done here The pod closes and is lifted back to the track. Move along the line to follow it to the next machine.
handle.travel: On the track Pods ride an overhead track from machine to machine. Much of a wafer's time in the factory is spent travelling and waiting its turn, not being worked on.
handle.ship: To another plant Between plants, pods and trays travel packed in crates, by truck or by plane, often to another country.
handle.ingot: To the saw The finished crystal is ground perfectly round and taken to be sliced.
handle.into: Into the pod A robot slides your finished wafer into a sealed pod. From here on it is carried by machines, never touched by hand.
handle.start: The journey starts The pod leaves for the chip factory, which is often in another place.
handle.loop: Round again Back to the start of the loop for the next layer. Your chip goes round about {layers} times.
handle.packed: Into a tray With its lid on, your finished chip is placed in a tray, to leave for its last test.
handle.trays: In trays Finished chips arrive in trays, one pocket each, to be tested one last time.
handle.out: Out Packed and labelled, the chips leave for the companies that build them into data centres, phones and cars.
proc.crystal.sand: Sand Silicon comes from quartz sand. It is purified until almost nothing but silicon is left.
proc.crystal.melt: Melt The pure silicon is melted in a quartz bowl, hotter than lava.
proc.crystal.pull: Pull A small seed crystal dips into the melt and is drawn slowly up, turning. Silicon freezes onto it as one perfect crystal, over a day or more.
proc.slice.saw: Saw Wires coated with diamond cut the crystal into hundreds of thin slices at once.
proc.slice.polish: Polish Each slice is ground and polished until it is flatter than almost anything people make: this is your wafer.
proc.clean: Wash The wafer spins while jets of ultrapure water and chemicals wash away specks and leftovers. Every new layer starts here.
proc.deposit: New film In the hot chamber, gases react on the wafer and leave a film over its whole surface, far thinner than a soap bubble.
proc.print.coat: Coat A drop of light-sensitive liquid is spun out into an even layer: it changes wherever light falls on it.
proc.print.expose: Print Light shines through the mask, the pattern of one layer, and lenses shrink it onto the wafer, one patch after another.
proc.print.develop: Develop A liquid washes away the parts the light touched. What is left is a stencil for the next machine.
proc.etch: Etch In vacuum, a glowing gas of charged particles (plasma) cuts the film straight down wherever the stencil leaves it bare. Then the stencil is stripped away.
proc.implant.beam: Implant Atoms of another element are given a charge, sped up, sorted by a magnet and shot into the bare silicon. They change how it conducts.
proc.implant.heat: Heal A flash of heat, far shorter than a second, lets the shaken crystal settle and the new atoms take their places.
proc.wires.plate: Copper In a bath, an electric current grows copper into every cut, and over everything else too.
proc.wires.polish: Polish flat Pressed onto a turning pad with a fine slurry, the extra copper is polished away. Copper is left only in the cuts: wires.
proc.test: Test A card of fine needles touches each chip in turn and runs it. The map fills in: green works, red does not.
proc.pkg.saw: Cut A thin turning blade, or a laser, cuts the wafer into separate chips.
proc.pkg.pick: Pick A head picks up a chip the map marked good, and flips it face down.
proc.pkg.bond: Join Tiny solder bumps join the chip to its package base, which carries signals and power out to the board.
proc.ship.test: Last test Pressed into a socket, each packaged chip is tested once more, often hot and cold.
proc.ship.pack: Pack Chips are sorted by how fast they run and packed for the companies that ordered them.
slice.title: your wafer, cut open
what.handle.track: Carries sealed boxes of wafers from machine to machine, all through the factory.
what.handle.filters: Filters across the whole ceiling push clean air down, carrying dust away from the wafers.
lens.title: under the lens: your wafer
lens.crystal: Silicon atoms from the melt settle onto the crystal, each one in line with the atoms below it. One mistake in the rows and the crystal is no good.
lens.polish: Slurry and a turning pad grind the cut surface down until it is flat and smooth as a mirror.
lens.clean: Liquids wash over the surface and carry the specks away. A speck left here can ruin the chip printed over it.
lens.deposit: Gas flows over the hot wafer and leaves a film behind, a few atoms at a time, evenly everywhere.
lens.coat: A drop of light-sensitive liquid is spun out into an even stencil layer over the film.
lens.expose: Light passes only through the mask's openings. Where it lands, the stencil changes.
lens.develop: A liquid washes away the stencil where the light changed it, leaving openings down to the film.
lens.etch: Ions in the plasma strike straight down. They cut the film only where the stencil is open.
lens.implant: Atoms of another element are fired into the silicon through the openings. They change how it carries current.
lens.heat: A flash of heat lets the new atoms settle into the silicon's rows, where they can do their work.
lens.plate: Copper from the bath grows over everything, filling every cut.
lens.cmp: The pad polishes the copper back until it is left only in the cuts: these are the wires.
lens.probe: A needle touches each chip's pads, and the test head runs the chip for a moment.
lens.dice: The wafer is cut apart. Each good chip gets small balls of solder on its face.
lens.bond: The chip goes face down onto its package base. Heat melts the solder and joins them.
lens.final: In its package, the chip is tested again, hot and then cold, as it will be used.
lens.titleCrystal: under the lens: the crystal growing
route.any.wafers: Silicon crystals are grown in crucibles of ultra-pure quartz, then sliced and polished into wafers, mostly in Japan, Taiwan and Germany. Chemicals and some raw materials come from many more places.
route.any.tools: The fab's machines come from a few makers. EUV scanners come only from ASML in the Netherlands, built around German mirrors and lasers. Deposition, etch and inspection tools come from the United States and Japan.
route.datacentre.design: Engineers write down what the chip must do and design it, using processor cores licensed from others and design software from a few companies. The finished design goes to the fab as files, and the masks are made from them.
route.datacentre.fab: The accelerator's dies are made in Taiwan on the most advanced lines. Each wafer goes round the loop of steps once for every layer, for months.
route.datacentre.memory: Its memory is made in stacks, mostly in Korea, and shipped to where the chip is packaged. It is often the scarcest part.
route.datacentre.package: The dies and their memory stacks are joined side by side in one package, then tested.
route.datacentre.systems: The packages are built into boards, servers and whole racks, with cooling and networking, in Taiwan, in Mexico and, more and more, in the United States.
route.datacentre.use: The racks are switched on in a data centre and run day and night for years. From the first design to the first answer, the trip takes years and crosses many countries.
route.phone.design: Phone chips are designed by phone makers and chip companies in the United States, Taiwan, China and Korea, nearly all with processor cores licensed from Arm.
route.phone.fab: Most of them are made on the most advanced lines in Taiwan, some in Korea.
route.phone.package: Each chip is packaged, often with its memory stacked on top, and tested.
route.phone.assembly: The chip goes onto a phone's board with many others, and the phone is put together, mostly in China and more and more in India and Vietnam.
route.phone.use: The phone is in your hand for a few years, charged every day.
route.car.design: Car chips come mostly from companies in Europe, Japan and the United States that design and make their own chips and sell them to the makers of car parts.
route.car.tools: Most car chips are made on older, larger processes. They need no EUV: deep-ultraviolet scanners from the Netherlands and Japan print them.
route.car.fab: They are made in the chipmakers' own fabs in Germany, Japan and elsewhere, and at foundries in Taiwan. Many of these lines are decades old and still busy.
route.car.package: They are packaged and tested, often in Malaysia, and must pass harder tests than a phone's chips: heat, cold, shaking and years of use.
route.car.modules: Makers of car parts build them into control units for the brakes, the engine, the airbags and the screens.
route.car.use: A car carries dozens of these units for many years, in heat, cold and rain.
what.handle.queue: Pods waiting their turn for this machine. How many wait depends on how full the fab runs and on how busy this machine is: the busiest machines have the longest queues, and they set the pace of the whole fab.
station.check.when: every pattern, before anything is built
station.layout.when: cells in rows, wires on two layers
station.masks.when: one stencil per layer, to the factory
part.need.box: your chip, still a black box
what.need.box: So far only a promise: these inputs in, these outputs out, the right answer every time.
what.need.ins: The wires coming in. Each carries a 0 or a 1; the job must be done for every mix of them.
what.need.outs: The wires going out, with the answers the job wants.
what.need.use: What the answers mean outside the chip: a sum, a lamp, a digit on a display, a count, a result inside a processor.
what.logic.code: Lines of text, one per wire: & is AND, | is OR, ^ is XOR, ~ is NOT. reg makes a wire a flip-flop, which remembers between clock ticks. Real chips are described the same way, in languages such as Verilog, only far longer.
what.logic.table: Every pattern of inputs and the answer the job wants for it. With n inputs there are 2 to the power n patterns, which is why big chips cannot be checked this way alone.
what.check.waves: Each line is a wire over time, high for 1 and low for 0, one pattern after another. Where your design's answer differs from the job's, the wire is marked in red.
what.check.verdict: One mark for each pattern: right or wrong.
what.gates.cells: Small circuits from a library, each a few transistors: the program picked and joined them to do what your text says.
what.gates.pins: Where the inputs enter the gates. A lit wire carries a 1.
what.layout.tile: Your cells in rows, and the wires between them: metal across in one colour, metal up and down in the other, small squares where they meet through a via.
what.layout.shared: Many small designs on one chip, each on its own tile, all sharing the chip's pins: a selector chooses which one is connected. Sharing makes a real chip affordable for one person. The numbered tiles are designs people have already added.
what.masks.masks: The layout split into stencils, one per layer. Real chips need dozens; the newest, about a hundred.
what.masks.reticle: A plate of quartz with the pattern in chrome, larger than the chip: the scanner shrinks its image onto the wafer.
what.need.plan: Every piece the shared computer needs, joined to what needs it. Green: built and checked. Dashed: open, anyone can build it. Dotted: nothing here can check it yet; bringing an engine for it is a contribution too. The small figures say who built each piece: a person, an AI, or both.
what.block.yours: Your design from the studio, as it would sit in this block: rows of standard cells of the same kind as these, only larger, placed and wired by the same kind of program. The outline shows up to 40 of its cells.
here.title: Built by the community
here.chip: The community is building a small open computer on a shared chip, piece by piece, people and AI together: {built} of its {total} pieces are built. A chip like this one is built the same way, by far more people.
here.block: Your design, {job}, became {cells} cells of the same kind as these. A block like this holds hundreds of thousands or more, placed and wired by programs, as yours were.
here.gate: Your design, {job}, uses these cells: {list}. A cell is a ready-made logic gate or other small circuit. Each is built from two to a couple of dozen switches, drawn in layers like this gate.
here.switch: Your design, {job}, needs about {transistors} switches like this one.
here.see: See it inside a real chip: {depth} ({world})
debate.memory.q: AI chips do math faster than memory can feed them. Where will the next big jump in bandwidth come from?
debate.memory.v0.claim: Put memory on top of, or right beside, the compute: more HBM stacks, hybrid bonding, 3D chips.
debate.memory.v0.assumes: Heat can still escape from taller stacks, and stacked parts keep yielding well.
debate.memory.v1.claim: Spread SRAM across a wafer-sized chip so the weights never leave the silicon.
debate.memory.v1.assumes: Models fit in on-chip memory, or split across many such chips cheaply.
debate.memory.v2.claim: Smaller numbers, sparsity and computing inside memory cut the bytes that must move at all.
debate.memory.v2.assumes: Answers stay accurate enough at low precision.
debate.power.q: AI data centers ask for ever more electricity. What cuts the energy of an answer most?
debate.power.v0.claim: Each chip generation does much more work per watt; keep improving the hardware.
debate.power.v0.assumes: Process and architecture gains keep coming at the old pace.
debate.power.v1.claim: Smaller number formats and smaller models do the same job with a fraction of the work.
debate.power.v1.assumes: Quality holds as models and numbers shrink.
debate.power.v2.claim: Efficiency gains get used up by more demand; the real limit is how fast power plants and grids can grow.
debate.power.v2.assumes: Demand keeps rising whatever the chips do.
debate.shrink.q: Transistors are now stacked sheets. Where does progress come from next?
debate.shrink.v0.claim: Stacked CFET transistors and 2D-material channels keep density rising for another decade.
debate.shrink.v0.assumes: New materials and steps can be made at scale, at an affordable cost.
debate.shrink.v1.claim: Progress moves to packaging: chiplets, hybrid bonding and 3D stacks.
debate.shrink.v1.assumes: Links between dies become dense and cheap enough to behave like one chip.
debate.shrink.v2.claim: The big gains come from new kinds of computing, not from smaller switches.
debate.shrink.v2.assumes: New machines get the software and tools that today's chips have.
debate.designcost.t: The cost of designing a chip
debate.designcost.q: A leading-edge chip can cost hundreds of millions of dollars to design. How much of that can AI agents remove?
debate.designcost.v0.claim: Agents already write RTL, tests and scripts; design teams will shrink and costs fall sharply.
debate.designcost.v0.assumes: Checking an agent's work can be automated and trusted too.
debate.designcost.v1.claim: Writing was never the main cost; specification, verification and sign-off still need people, masks still cost money.
debate.designcost.v1.assumes: Judgment about what to build and what to trust stays hard to automate.
debate.open.q: Open software changed the world. Can an open instruction set, open tools and open PDKs do the same for chips?
debate.open.v0.claim: RISC-V, open tools and shared runs lower the cost of starting, so many more people can build chips.
debate.open.v0.assumes: A shared base of verified designs and tools keeps growing.
debate.open.v1.claim: Every attempt costs masks, fab time and testing; open designs do not remove the biggest costs or the need for trusted verification.
debate.supply.q: Most advanced chips pass through a few fabs and packaging lines. How should the chain be made resilient?
debate.supply.v0.claim: Build leading-edge fabs and packaging in more regions, so one shock cannot stop the world.
debate.supply.v0.assumes: Governments and customers will keep paying the higher cost.
debate.supply.v1.claim: Keep the efficient hubs and add stockpiles, second sources and long contracts.
debate.supply.v1.assumes: Shocks are short enough to ride out on buffers.
debate.signoff.q: If AI agents write most of a chip's code and tests, who is responsible when the silicon fails?
debate.signoff.v0.claim: An engineer must review and sign off; responsibility cannot be handed to a tool.
debate.signoff.v0.assumes: People can still understand and check what the agent built.
debate.signoff.v1.claim: Formal checks and coverage targets can certify an agent's work better than a tired reviewer.
debate.signoff.v1.assumes: The specification itself is complete and correct.
debate.paradigm.q: Many kinds of machine are being tried, each strong on different jobs. By 2040, will one kind win, or will computers be mixtures of many?
debate.paradigm.v0.claim: Digital chips like today's GPUs keep winning, because their software and tools are years ahead.
debate.paradigm.v0.assumes: Software and tooling matter more than raw efficiency.
debate.paradigm.v1.claim: Energy limits force mixtures: analog, optical, spiking and quantum parts each doing the job they suit.
debate.paradigm.v1.assumes: Software can split one program across very different machines.
debate.mature.q: Most chips by count come from older factories with thin margins, yet one missing part can stop a car line. Who should keep that capacity running?
debate.mature.v0.claim: After a shortage, buyers sign longer contracts and pay more for secure supply; prices do the work.
debate.mature.v0.assumes: Buyers remember shortages long enough to pay for safety.
debate.mature.v1.claim: A shortage costs far more than keeping spare capacity, so public support or shared reserves make sense.
debate.mature.v1.assumes: Support can be targeted without propping up the wrong factories.
debate.quantum.q: When will quantum computers do useful work that ordinary computers cannot?
debate.quantum.v0.claim: Reliable qubits have started to beat raw ones, and companies plan fault-tolerant machines within a few years.
debate.quantum.v0.assumes: Errors and overhead keep falling as machines grow.
debate.quantum.v1.claim: Better classical methods have challenged several advantage claims, and approximate methods already work well for many molecules.
debate.quantum.v1.assumes: Useful problems keep enough structure for classical shortcuts.
debate.bigdie.q: Bigger chips catch more defects. When does splitting a design into chiplets win?
debate.bigdie.v0.claim: Small dies yield better, can mix processes and can be reused across products.
debate.bigdie.v0.assumes: Die-to-die links are fast, cheap and low-power enough.
debate.bigdie.v1.claim: Keeping everything on one huge piece of silicon avoids slow links; spare cores route around defects.
debate.bigdie.v1.assumes: Redundancy and cooling can handle a wafer-sized chip.
debate.skills.q: When AI writes code and layouts, what will chip engineers spend their time on? Which skills last?
debate.skills.v0.claim: People set goals, review agents' work and decide trade-offs; tool-specific skills matter less.
debate.skills.v0.assumes: Agents become reliable enough to trust with whole steps.
debate.skills.v1.claim: Someone has to know why a design fails; deep knowledge of physics, timing and verification grows in value.
debate.skills.v1.assumes: Agents keep making subtle mistakes that only experts catch.

way.title: Another way to compute
way.note: A judgment, not a measurement: where things stand changes fast.
way.add: Add a way, or correct this one
way.saves.energy: the energy each step of computing costs
way.saves.data: the cost of moving data, not computing with it
way.super.how: In metals cooled close to absolute zero, current flows with no resistance at all. Logic built from them switches with tiny pulses of magnetic flux, and wastes almost nothing.
way.super.catch: Everything must be kept colder than outer space, the circuits are far less dense than today's, and the cooling costs energy of its own.
way.super.now: Teams are designing such chips for AI data centres, betting the savings outweigh the cooling.
way.photonic.how: Light carries data between chips without heating the wires, and beams that interfere can do a whole matrix of multiply-adds as they pass.
way.photonic.catch: Turning electrical numbers into light and back costs energy and precision, and light is hard to store.
way.photonic.now: Light already carries data between racks and is moving onto the package; light that computes is still early.
way.spatial.how: Instead of fetching numbers from memory chips, the whole program is laid out across a very large chip, each tile keeping its numbers beside it, and data flows from tile to tile.
way.spatial.catch: A model must fit in the chip's own memory, and a chip the size of a wafer needs its own answers to defects, power and heat.
way.spatial.now: Sold today for AI, where its makers lead on speed for each user.
way.approx.how: Use fewer bits where nobody notices the small errors: AI models run well on numbers of 8, 4 or even fewer bits, and a smaller number is cheaper to move and multiply.
way.approx.catch: It only works where errors are tolerable, and someone must check that they are.
way.neuro.how: Like neurons, its parts send a spike only when something changes, and spend almost nothing while nothing happens.
way.neuro.catch: Most software is not written for spikes, and training spiking networks is still hard.
way.neuro.now: Research chips and small products that listen or watch all the time on a tiny battery.
way.analog.how: Voltages stand for numbers, and a circuit solves an equation continuously instead of step by step.
way.analog.catch: Noise limits precision, and each problem needs the circuit rewired.
way.analog.now: Small companies sell analog computers again, for control and for solving equations.
way.cim.how: Do the multiply-adds inside the memory cells, where the numbers are stored, so they never travel over the busy wires.
way.cim.catch: Analog cells drift and differ from one another, and big models outgrow the arrays.
way.cim.now: Prototype and early product chips, mostly for small AI models.
way.reversible.how: Logic that throws no information away does not have to pay the floor for erasing it, and the energy of a switch can be recycled instead of turned into heat.
way.reversible.catch: It is slower, needs more transistors, and a whole computer built this way has never been made.
way.reversible.now: Test chips, and a few companies starting to build them.
way.pbits.how: Bits that flicker between 0 and 1 on purpose, made from switches too small to sit still. Wired together, they settle into good answers to search and sampling problems.
way.pbits.catch: Only some problems fit, and making the noise behave is an engineering problem of its own.
way.quantum.how: Qubits hold many possibilities at once, and interference steers them toward answers some problems need, such as simulating molecules.
way.quantum.catch: Qubits lose their state at the slightest disturbance; useful machines need error correction, with many physical qubits for every reliable one.
way.quantum.now: Prototype machines; error-corrected ones are the race now.

field.pinhead.q: What stops us writing a whole library on a pinhead?
field.pinhead.opened: The idea of building things atom by atom.
field.pinhead.open: The smallest parts are now counted in atoms.
field.heat.q: Must thinking make heat at all?
field.heat.opened: Erasing a bit has a smallest possible heat.
field.heat.open: Chips still run far above that floor. Could chips that never erase get near it?
field.nature.q: Can a computer copy nature exactly?
field.brain.q: How does a brain think so well with slow, sloppy parts?
field.brain.open: No chip yet learns on a brain's power.
field.dark.q: Why must most of a chip go dark?
field.dark.opened: Power, not space, is what limits a chip.
field.dark.open: What to build in the parts that cannot all be on at once.
field.wires.q: How do you join a million parts without a million wires?
field.wires.opened: The integrated circuit: the wires made together with the parts.
field.wires.open: Wires limit chips again, now between the pieces in one package.
field.wear.q: Why does a chip that never moves wear out?
field.wear.opened: Designing every wire to last a lifetime.
field.wear.open: Thinner wires carrying the same current wear out faster.
field.spare.q: Can the whole be more reliable than every one of its parts?
field.spare.opened: Error correction, and spare parts inside the chip.
field.spare.open: As parts get smaller and noisier, how much spare is enough?
field.palm.q: Why does your phone slow down while you hold it?
field.palm.who: Phone chip makers such as Qualcomm, 2013
field.palm.opened: Chips that move work to cooler, slower cores.
field.palm.open: Phones now run AI, but your hand still sets the limit.
field.life.q: How sure must a chip be when a life depends on it?
field.life.who: ISO 26262, the standard for car safety, 2011
field.life.opened: Chips that check themselves while they drive.
field.life.open: Driving by itself needs the fastest chips, and the fastest are the least proven.
field.fetch.q: Why does fetching a number cost far more than using it?
field.fetch.opened: Computing next to the memory, or inside it.
field.fetch.open: Many AI chips spend more energy moving data than computing with it.
field.wait.q: If the chip gets faster, why does it spend more time waiting?
field.wait.opened: The memory wall, and memory stacked beside the chip.
field.wait.open: Memory, not computing, is now the main limit for AI.
field.secret.q: How can a chip that does exactly what it should still give away secrets?
field.secret.opened: Timing became part of what correct means.
field.secret.open: A definition of correct that includes time.
field.lid.q: Why did a chip's own package flip its bits?
field.lid.opened: Purer materials, and memory that corrects itself.
field.lid.open: Smaller charges are easier to flip.
field.perfect.who: Since Carver Mead and Lynn Conway, 1979
field.perfect.opened: Design rules that hide the factory from the designer.
field.perfect.open: What the rules hide leaks through more at every shrink.
field.copy.q: Why copy even what nobody understands?
field.copy.opened: New factories matched to the old one, down to the air pressure.
field.copy.open: Can a factory's know-how ever be written down?
field.pins.q: How do you check billions of parts through a few hundred pins?
field.pins.opened: Scan: chains that let a tester read every switch inside.
field.pins.open: Chips stacked in layers hide their middle from every pin.
field.later.q: Why does a chip that passed every test compute wrong years later?
field.later.opened: Hunting silent errors across whole fleets of machines.
field.later.open: How to catch a fault that shows up only now and then.
field.trust.q: Can you trust a chip you didn't make, even after checking every line?
field.trust.opened: Trust in the whole chain, from tools to factory.
field.trust.open: Hidden changes in hardware, and in designs made by AI.
field.package.q: Why were AI chips short when there were enough chips?
field.package.opened: The package became a factory of its own.
field.package.open: Joining pieces in one package is now as hard as making them.
field.oxen.q: Two strong oxen or a thousand chickens?
field.oxen.opened: The race between a few fast cores and many simple ones.
field.oxen.open: The chickens won for AI. Will it last?
field.fabless.q: Does a chip company need its own factory?
field.fabless.opened: Foundries, and chip design without a factory.
field.fabless.open: Now so few factories make the most advanced chips.
field.printer.q: Should the whole world rely on one maker of the printing machine?
field.printer.who: Since the first EUV machines shipped, 2017
field.printer.opened: One machine became the narrowest point of all chipmaking.
field.printer.open: Whether a second way to print the smallest parts can exist.
field.anyone.q: Can someone who never enters a factory design a chip?
field.anyone.opened: Students designing real chips, and a whole design industry.
field.anyone.open: Open tools and shared runs, so anyone can try.
field.cheaper.q: Why does putting more on a chip make each part cheaper, until it doesn't?
field.cheaper.opened: Moore's law, which was about cost from the start.
field.cheaper.open: Whether each part keeps getting cheaper.
field.general.q: One chip for everything, or one chip for each job?
field.general.who: Ted Hoff, 1969; John Hennessy and David Patterson, 2018
field.general.opened: The microprocessor, then special chips again, with open instruction sets like RISC-V.
field.general.open: How special a chip can be before it is too narrow.
field.lottery.q: Did the best idea win, or the one that fit the chips?
field.lottery.opened: Seeing that hardware decides which ideas succeed.
field.lottery.open: Which ideas today's AI chips are hiding.
field.scale.q: Why does more computing keep beating clever ideas?
field.scale.open: What happens when computing stops getting cheaper.
field.top.q: When there's no room left at the bottom, where is it?
field.top.opened: Gains from better software, algorithms and chip design.
field.top.open: Who does that work, and how.
field.prove.who: After Thomas Nicely found a division bug in the Pentium, 1994
field.prove.opened: Proving parts of a chip correct by machine, not only testing them.
field.prove.open: Proofs cover parts of a chip; testing still covers the rest.
field.onebad.q: Why can one bad piece throw away four good ones?
field.onebad.who: Makers of chips in several pieces, since the 1990s
field.onebad.opened: Testing every piece before it is joined: the known good die.
field.onebad.open: Pieces stacked on top of each other can't all be tested first.
field.dollar.q: Why can a car wait months for a chip that costs a dollar?
field.dollar.opened: Car makers learning where their chips really come from.
field.dollar.open: Cars need more chips every year, most of them made on older lines.

field.purity.open: Every new chip asks for fewer stray atoms, and only a few firms can make silicon that pure.
field.mask.q: Why does a mask look nothing like the chip it prints?

field.mask.opened: Optical proximity correction: masks bent in advance, so light bends them back.

field.oxide.open: Every layer is now a few atoms thick; which material comes next?

field.quartz.open: Whether synthetic quartz or other mines can take over before the next storm.
field.neon.q: Why can a war far away stop the gas a chip printer's laser needs?

field.neon.opened: Chipmakers recycling neon and buying it from more places.
field.neon.open: Every rare gas and metal has its own few suppliers.
field.station.q: Why does a building full of chips now need a power station of its own?

field.station.open: Whether new power can be built as fast as new chips.
field.jevons.q: When each answer takes less energy, why does the world use more?

field.jevons.opened: Seeing that cheaper computing finds new uses faster than it saves.
field.jevons.open: Whether efficiency alone can ever bring the total down.

field.batch.open: How to keep each person fast when the chip is full, and who waits.

seek.phoneboard.soc: The processor makes most of the board's heat, in a spot about the size of a fingernail.
seek.phoneboard.pmic: The power chip warms too: each change of voltage loses a little energy as heat.
seek.phoneboard.modem: The modem works hardest when the signal is weak, and gets warmer then.
seek.phoneboard.storage: Storage draws power mostly while it reads or writes, so it often stays the coolest chip here.
seek.gate.find: Find what decides which rule this gate follows.
seek.gate.gates: Each switch gate is one input. It crosses both silicon strips, so it turns one switch on and another off.
seek.gate.diff: The two silicon strips hold two kinds of switch: one kind turns on with a high voltage, the other with a low.
seek.gate.metal: The switches here are the same kinds as in every other gate. What differs is how these wires join them.
seek.campus.find: Find where the electricity comes in.
seek.campus.halls: Each hall is full of racks and has its own cooling and power, so a campus can grow one hall at a time.
seek.campus.cooling: The machines on the roofs carry heat away. Nearly all the electricity that comes in leaves again as heat.
seek.campus.substation: Here the grid's high voltage is stepped down for the halls. Everything on this campus runs on what comes in here.
seek.hall.find: Find what ties these racks to each other.
seek.hall.racks: Row after row of the same cabinet, each full of computers built alike.
seek.hall.hotaisle: Cold air goes in at the fronts of the racks and comes out hot at the back, into this closed aisle.
seek.hall.trays: The network's cables run in these trays, from rack to rack. They are what let many machines share one job.
seek.rack.find: Find where the calculating is done.
seek.rack.switch: Every server in the rack is cabled to this switch, and through it to the rest of the hall.
seek.rack.servers: Each shelf is a computer built around a few large chips. This is where the calculating happens.
seek.rack.power: The hall's electricity becomes the low, steady voltage the boards need here. Every server above draws on it.
seek.board.find: Find where this board's sums are done.
seek.board.package: The chip that does the sums sits in this package. Everything else on the board feeds it power or numbers.
seek.board.lid: The metal lid protects the chip and spreads its heat into the heat sink that sat on top.
seek.board.powerstages: Each of these small blocks turns the board's supply into the very low voltage the chip runs on. There are many, because the chip draws so much current.
seek.accel.die: Copies of one compute tile, side by side. Each copy does the same steps on different numbers.
seek.accel.hbm: Each tower is memory chips stacked on top of each other, set right beside the die so numbers have only a short way to travel.
seek.accel.base: The die and the memory towers stand on one base. Layers of wiring inside it join them, and carry every connection out to the board.
seek.handset.find: Find where the day's energy comes in.
seek.handset.screen: When it is lit, the screen spends more of the battery than any other part. Most of the day it is dark, and the chips inside go on working.
seek.handset.antenna: The radio keeps in touch with the network even while the phone sleeps, and works harder when the signal is weak.
seek.handset.cable: Everything the phone did today came out of one battery. This cable fills it again, usually overnight.
seek.chip.find: Find the blocks that do the work.
seek.chip.cores: Each compute block fetches numbers, calculates and passes results on. None of them sees the whole job.
seek.chip.cache: Memory on the chip itself. A number kept here arrives far sooner than one from the memory outside.
seek.chip.io: Every number the chip works on comes in, and every result goes out, through these circuits at its edge.
seek.chip.clock: One tick, carried on these wires to every part, keeps the whole chip in step.
seek.phone.board: All the phone's computing is on this one small board, at the top. Most of the rest is battery.
seek.phone.battery: The battery fills most of the phone. Every other part has to fit around it.
seek.phone.camera: The lenses gather light and the sensor records it. What the photo finally looks like is worked out afterwards, by the chip.
seek.phone.antenna: Parts of the metal frame are the antennas: the case itself reaches out to the network.
seek.soc.find: Find the district built for the sums AI needs.
seek.soc.cpu: Big cores and small ones: the phone moves work between them, to save energy when the work is light.
seek.soc.gpu: Many small, identical cores that draw the screen's pictures, all working at once.
seek.soc.npu: This district does the multiplications AI needs, many at a time, for less energy than the other cores would use.
seek.soc.isp: The camera unit gets the picture first, straight from the sensor, before any other district sees it.
seek.soc.cache: Every district reads and writes here, so work can pass from one to another without leaving the chip.
seek.car.controllers: Small computers sit all over the car, in hot places and cold ones, each in charge of one job.
seek.car.wiring: Cables carry power and messages between the control units, through the whole car.
seek.car.sensors: Cameras and radar watch the road and pass what they see to the computers.
seek.car.battery: The floor of the car is its battery, and a control unit of its own watches every cell.
seek.car.motor: The inverter beside the motor switches large currents on and off, many thousands of times a second.
seek.car.wheels: Everything the computers decide ends here, as braking, steering and turning wheels.
seek.ecu.mcu: This small chip makes every decision in the unit, running the same program again and again.
seek.ecu.connector: Every signal from the car's sensors, and every command out, passes through this plug.
seek.ecu.drivers: These big switches carry the real current. They do only what the small chip tells them.
seek.mcu.find: Find where the program is run.
seek.mcu.cores: Two cores do the same work in step. If their answers ever differ, something has gone wrong.
seek.mcu.flash: The program lives here, and stays when the car is switched off.
seek.mcu.sram: The numbers being worked on right now live here, and are lost when the power goes.
seek.mcu.periph: Signals from the sensors arrive here and become numbers the cores can use.
seek.scanner.find: Find where the light is made.
seek.scanner.source: A laser hits drops of molten tin, and the flash of light it makes is what prints the chip.
seek.scanner.mirrors: This light is swallowed by glass, so there are no lenses here: only mirrors, polished extremely smooth.
seek.scanner.mask: The pattern of one layer, drawn larger than it will be printed, like a stencil.
seek.scanner.stage: The wafer moves under the light and stops at each chip in turn, exactly in place.
seek.scanner.vacuum: This light cannot travel through air, so the inside of the machine is pumped empty.
seek.die.find: Find the part that does your chip's work.
seek.die.cores: Your chip's cores: the same pattern on every chip of this wafer.
seek.die.pads: Small metal squares round the edge: the only way in or out for every signal.
seek.die.probes: Needles touch the pads and test the chip while it is still on the wafer.
seek.die.scribe: The lane between chips. A saw will cut along it, and nothing here is kept.
seek.block.cells: Every standard cell in a row has the same height, so a program can line them up like books on a shelf.
seek.block.sram: Each cell of this grid holds one bit, and only for as long as the power stays on.
seek.block.wires: The wires run on many layers above the cells, so they can cross each other without touching.
seek.switch.find: Find the part that turns this switch on and off.
seek.switch.gate: Its voltage decides whether current crosses the sheets. It controls the flow without joining it.
seek.switch.channel: The current flows through these thin sheets of silicon, with the gate wrapped around them on every side.
seek.switch.oxide: This skin is so thin that the gate's voltage acts straight through it, yet almost no current crosses it.
seek.switch.source: The moving charges enter the sheets here. Source and drain look alike: which is which is set by the voltages on them, not by their shape.
seek.switch.drain: The charges leave the sheets here and go on through the wires above.
seek.atom.lattice: Each silicon atom holds on to four neighbours, in the same pattern over and over.
seek.atom.dopant: One atom of another element among the silicon. Its spare electron, or the one it lacks, is what lets current flow here.
seek.atom.electrons: The electrons drift from atom to atom, and that drift is the current.
seek.atom.boundary: Close up, the switch's insulating skin is only a few rows of atoms. Electrons can slip through a wall that thin.
joule.q: One answer from an AI costs energy. Where does it all go, and how far down could we bring it?
joule.job: One answer from a 70-billion-parameter language model, 500 words long: a multiply-add for every weight for every word.
joule.pulled: {lever}: the whole answer changed by {v}%, and so did every level below and above.
joule.other: The other sides it pays on: {s} s for an answer, and an accuracy of {db} dB.
joule.keep: Keep this plan as an attempt
joule.here: of one answer go here, at the {level}
joule.at.building: Pumping out the heat and converting power. It pays for everything below it once more.
joule.at.rack: The network between machines: every answer's numbers cross it.
joule.at.board: Fetching the model's weights from memory for every word, and the host machine around the chip.
joule.at.chip: Moving numbers through the chip's own memory, on their way from far memory to the blocks.
joule.at.block: Reading the two numbers of every multiply-add from registers right beside it; with compute in memory, summing them in the arrays instead.
joule.at.gate: The arithmetic itself: the only part the answer needs.
joule.at.switch: Current that leaks through switches that are off, for as long as the answer takes.
joule.at.atom: The least physics asks for: the bits the arithmetic erases, at room temperature.
joule.lever.home.d: Memory chips on the board, stacks of memory beside the chip in its package, or the whole model in on-chip memory.
joule.lever.batch.d: Each weight fetched is used once for every user served at the same time.
joule.lever.precision.d: Fewer bits move fewer bytes and need smaller multipliers, and add rounding noise.
joule.lever.clock.t: Clock, at the lowest voltage that runs
joule.lever.clock.d: A slower clock runs at a lower voltage; below the lowest voltage, leakage takes over.
joule.lever.cim.d: Sum the weights inside the memory arrays where they are stored, with converters at the edge.
joule.lever.adcBits.d: How finely the arrays' sums are read back: each bit doubles the converters' energy.
joule.lever.pue.d: Power use effectiveness: the building's energy over the machines'. Liquid cooling brings it nearer 1.
joule.lever.optics.d: Plugged-in optical modules, or optics packaged beside the switch chip.
joule.map.aria: {n} attempts, by the energy of one answer against the time it takes. Yours is the ring.
joule.map.d: Each dot is an attempt, by its energy (down is less) and its time (left is quicker). The large dots are on the frontier: nothing beats them on energy, time and accuracy at once. Your plan is the ring.
joule.map.none: No attempts in the ledger yet. Yours can be the first.
joule.model: The budget engine, on a 45 nm ruler: the shares and the directions hold, the joules are for comparing ideas. Nobody votes; the engine scores every attempt.
joule.offer.d: This question runs through a puzzle: where does the energy of one answer go, level by level?
joule.no.job: The job needs operations, bytes and reuse as numbers.
joule.no.home: Where the weights live: on the board (dram), beside the chip (hbm) or on the chip (sram).
joule.no.precision: Bits per number: fp16, fp8 or fp4.
joule.no.clock: The clock must be between 0.5 and 4.5 GHz.
joule.no.volt: The voltage must be between 0.5 and 1.1 V, and high enough for the clock.
joule.no.batch: Users served together: a whole number from 1 to 4,096.
joule.no.cim: Compute in memory is on (true) or off (false).
joule.no.pue: The hall's power use effectiveness: from 1 to 3.
joule.no.optics: Optics between machines: plug or cpo.
joule.more.levers: The levels and the levers here
curve.ui.title: How fast do ideas get better here?
curve.ui.lead: Every attempt someone keeps for this need joins the curve, in order: each dot is one attempt, and the line is the best energy so far. Nobody votes; the engine scores each one.
curve.ui.none: No attempt at this need has been kept yet. Yours would be the first point.
curve.ui.noLaw: {n} attempts so far. With three, and one that beats the first, the curve has a law.
curve.ui.law: Each time the attempts double, the best falls to {x} of what it was.
curve.ui.pace: At the pace of your machine, {tries} tries a year, doubling the {n} attempts so far alone would take {time}.
curve.ui.paceNever: Your machine rests on a try whose days are not known, so nobody can say how fast it moves the curve.
curve.ui.many: That is why it is a lab: many people and many agents, each trying in parallel, double the attempts much faster than one.
curve.law.moore: Moore's law counts years: the switches on a chip double every two years or so, and keeping that pace now takes more than 18 times the researchers of the early 1970s.
curve.law.wright: Wright's law counts things made: cost falls by a share each time the total made doubles. Tested on 62 technologies, it forecast best, with Moore's law close behind.
curve.law.lab: This curve counts attempts: the best design falls each time the attempts double. More attempts, faster tries, more ideas.
curve.ui.keepLead: It joins the curve at once, as yours. To put it in the ledger, open it on GitHub as a new file in a pull request.
curve.ui.cannot: Make a machine that follows the grammar and meets its need, and it can join the curve.
frame.q.perfect.hint: copies that differ, and the ones that fail
frame.q.dig.hint: how a clean 1 is made from a messy world
frame.q.vn.hint: spares, votes and codes that keep it right
frame.q.sutton.hint: search and learning against clever design
frame.q.moore.hint: smaller and cheaper, and what stops it
frame.q.line.hint: what is fixed, and what can change
frame.q.trust.hint: what is checked, and what nobody can check
frame.q.physics.hint: noise, heat and atoms: an enemy or a tool
frame.q.eff.hint: where the energy goes, and what saving it does
frame.q.nat.hint: what nature computes, and what nothing can
frame.q.copy.hint: where memory sits, and what can be copied
frame.meet.moore.perfect.q: As every switch shrinks toward a few atoms, can copies stay alike enough to be called the same design?
frame.meet.moore.perfect.open: How small a part can still be made as a copy, rather than as a one-off?
frame.meet.eff.geo.q: If fetching a number costs more than using it, should the work move to the data, instead of the data to the work?
frame.meet.eff.geo.open: What else would move the front? Every attempt kept in the ledger is a point on this chart, placed by the model; keep yours below.
frame.meet.eff.geo.true: Packing the logic beside the memory shortens every trip but piles up the heat: in this model, every point on the line is one of today's best compromises.
frame.meet.moore.physics.q: When a part is a few dozen atoms long, does shrinking it further still make it better?
frame.meet.moore.physics.open: Which physical effect ends shrinking first, and can any design work around it?
frame.meet.geo.line.q: Should a job sit where its data is, even if that means building a part only that job can use?
frame.meet.geo.line.open: How far from its data can a general part sit before a special one wins?
frame.meet.human.sutton.q: When a search designs a part no person could follow, who is its designer?
frame.meet.human.sutton.open: What part of designing should stay with people, and why?
frame.meet.human.moore: who can afford to make chips
frame.meet.human.moore.q: If every new generation costs more to make, how many people will still be able to make chips at all?
frame.meet.human.moore.open: Can shared runs, open tools or smaller fabs keep chip making open to many?
frame.meet.dig.line: logic is how you wire it
frame.meet.dig.line.q: If the same switches wired differently make different logic, where does the meaning of a circuit live?
frame.meet.dig.line.open: How much of a chip could be rewired after it is made, and what would that cost?
frame.meet.perfect.vn.q: Is it better to make each part good enough, or to make many poor parts that outvote each other?
frame.meet.perfect.vn.open: Where is the line between paying for margins and paying for spares?
frame.meet.human.line: who decides what a chip is for
frame.meet.human.line.q: Who decides what a chip is for, and what happens when the job changes after it is made?
frame.meet.human.line.open: How could the people who use a chip have a say in what it is built to do?
frame.meet.geo.moore: up when you cannot go smaller
frame.meet.geo.moore.q: When parts cannot get smaller, is stacking them upward the same kind of progress?
frame.meet.geo.moore.open: What limits stacking first: the heat, the wires between layers, or the cost?
frame.meet.human.trust.q: Would open records of how a chip was designed and made be enough to trust it?
frame.meet.human.trust.open: What would a record have to hold for strangers to rely on it?
frame.meet.dig.physics.q: How much noise could a computer live with if it stopped insisting on a clean 1?
frame.meet.dig.physics.open: Which answers could be a little wrong without anyone being harmed?
frame.meet.dig.physics.true: A 1 is only a voltage above a line: heat shakes the wire, and a bigger swing keeps the 1 clean at the price of energy. The chain draws the shaking far larger than in a real chip, where heat turns bits wrong mostly by making signals late.
frame.meet.eff.line.q: A part built for one job wastes less energy on it. Is that worth losing every other job?
frame.meet.eff.line.open: How special can a chip become before too few jobs are left for it?
frame.meet.nat.physics.q: If physical law can compute some answers by itself, which answers still need logic?
frame.meet.nat.physics.open: Which problems could a piece of matter solve faster than any program?
frame.meet.geo.perfect.q: When packing parts closer heats them, how much of the difference between copies is heat?
frame.meet.geo.perfect.open: How close can parts pack before the heat makes their copies too unlike?
frame.meet.copy.physics.q: If the memory itself does the computing, what is left to copy: the program, or the chip?
frame.meet.copy.physics.open: Where should the line between the two ways fall in a real chip, and who decides it?
frame.meet.copy.physics.true: Exact bits in an array, sums done by gates, copy perfectly; weights kept in each cell, sums made by currents meeting on a wire, cost far less energy but come out a little different on every chip, and from one run to the next.
frame.meet.nat.sutton.q: For a problem whose work doubles with every item, is searching harder ever enough?
frame.meet.nat.sutton.open: Which hard problems have given way to search, and which never could?
frame.meet.sutton.trust: checking a designer you cannot follow
frame.meet.sutton.trust.q: How do you check a designer whose reasons you cannot follow?
frame.meet.sutton.trust.open: What tests would show a searched design is right without understanding it?
frame.meet.perfect.trust.q: If every copy differs a little, what can a test of a few copies say about the rest?
frame.meet.perfect.trust.open: How many faults reach people because no test was built to find them?
frame.meet.trust.vn.q: Should you prove a design right once, or build it so a fault does not matter?
frame.meet.trust.vn.open: Which parts of a chip are worth proving, and which only worth doubling?
frame.meet.line.moore.q: When shrinking slows, is building special chips the new way to get faster?
frame.meet.line.moore.open: What will make chips better when neither shrinking nor specialising is enough?
frame.meet.line.sutton.q: Does a general chip that runs every new idea beat a clever one built for today's?
frame.meet.line.sutton.open: How long does a special chip stay useful while the ideas it was built for change?
frame.meet.copy.geo.q: If memory sits far from the logic and the logic keeps waiting, should memory move inside it?
frame.meet.copy.geo.open: How much memory can sit inside the logic before the logic has no room to work?
frame.meet.copy.geo.true: The farther the memory sits from the logic, the longer every number's trip, and the more of the logic's time is spent waiting, unless it has other work to do meanwhile.
frame.meet.eff.moore.q: If each switch keeps getting cheaper to run, why does the world use more energy on them?
frame.meet.eff.moore.open: What would make cheaper switches mean less energy in total?
frame.meet.eff.physics.q: Running slower at a lower voltage saves energy. When is waiting worth it?
frame.meet.eff.physics.open: How low can the voltage go before the noise wins?
frame.meet.eff.physics.true: Switching energy grows with the square of the voltage, so a lower voltage saves energy, if the chip can wait for the slower switch.
frame.meet.copy.dig.q: If remembering is a loop that holds a value, is memory just logic that never lets go?
frame.meet.copy.dig.open: Which kinds of memory could also compute, and what would they forget?
frame.meet.copy.dig.true: Two NOT gates feeding each other in a ring hold whichever value was last pushed into them: that is a bit of memory.
frame.meet.eff.sutton.q: If bigger models keep winning, is their energy the price of being clever?
frame.meet.eff.sutton.open: Can a model get better without getting bigger, and what would show it?
frame.meet.copy.eff: twenty watts and a power plant
frame.meet.copy.eff.q: A brain runs on about the power of a light bulb. What does it do that a chip does not?
frame.meet.copy.eff.open: Which of the brain's tricks could a chip use without having to learn like a brain?
frame.meet.copy.eff.true: Moving a number costs far more energy than adding with it, so where a machine keeps its memory decides what each answer costs.
frame.meet.perfect.physics.q: When a few atoms out of place change how a switch behaves, can any two switches be the same?
frame.meet.perfect.physics.open: How could a design use the differences between copies instead of fighting them?
frame.meet.dig.vn.q: Is a clean 1 better made by a bigger swing on one wire, or by several noisy wires voting?
frame.meet.dig.vn.open: Where does voting cost less energy than a bigger swing?
frame.meet.copy.vn.q: Should a damaged chip stop, or keep going and get a little worse, as a brain does?
frame.meet.copy.vn.open: Which jobs could live with a chip that fails slowly instead of all at once?
frame.meet.copy.nat.q: Could living cells compute, and could their answers be copied?
frame.meet.copy.nat.open: What can a living computer do that silicon cannot, and what would it cost to keep it alive?
frame.marks.say: Every mark on the picture is a question that lives here. Tap one to look through it.
frame.lens.pick: Look at this level through one of them. The picture lights what it is about.
frame.lens.none: No question lives at this level yet. What would you ask here?
frame.at.line.building.q: One hall, thousands of machines, rearranged by software every day. Which parts should be fixed, and which should keep changing?
frame.at.line.building.note: The jobs and the network of a hall are rearranged by software all the time; the chips inside are fixed the day they are made.
frame.at.perfect.building.q: Every chip here passed its tests. Why are some of them quietly giving wrong answers?
frame.at.perfect.building.note: Meta found about one silicon device in a thousand in its fleet computing wrong answers without any warning.
frame.at.eff.rack.q: Halve the power of every server and the hall fills with more servers. Where does the saving go?
frame.at.eff.rack.note: For every joule a chip uses, the server and the building around it use more: fans, power conversion and cooling.
frame.at.geo.rack.q: Pack more accelerators into one rack and they talk faster, and cook each other. How close is too close?
frame.at.geo.rack.note: Many racks for AI now carry so much heat that air cannot remove it, and liquid is brought to the chips.
frame.at.eff.board.q: Most of an answer's energy is spent on this board, fetching numbers from memory. Make it cheaper, and what happens to the total?
frame.at.eff.board.note: In the energy puzzle, moving data across the board is the largest share of one AI answer's energy.
frame.at.perfect.board.q: The same board, built a million times. Which copy fails first, and why?
frame.at.perfect.board.note: Chip and board grow by different amounts as they warm, and the joints between them flex every time.
frame.at.geo.chip.q: The memory sits a few millimetres from the chip, and every number the cores use has to make that trip. Is the trip the real cost?
frame.at.geo.chip.note: Reading 16 bits from memory chips costs about 3,500 times the energy of a 16-bit add, on a 45 nm chip.
frame.at.eff.chip.q: Make each answer cheaper and people ask for more. On this chip, what is the energy of one answer spent on?
frame.at.eff.chip.note: Most of an AI answer's energy goes to fetching the model's numbers from memory, not to the arithmetic.
frame.at.physics.block.q: Sum the numbers where they are stored, as currents in a memory array. Let physics do the arithmetic, noise and all?
frame.at.physics.block.note: Compute in memory multiplies each input by the weight stored in place and adds the results on a wire; its catch is noise, and converters that cost more for every bit.
frame.at.eff.block.q: Slow the clock and lower the voltage with it, and the chip draws half the power while still doing three quarters of the work. What will the saving be spent on?
frame.at.eff.block.note: Switching energy grows with the square of the voltage, and a slower clock can run at a lower voltage.
frame.at.dig.gate.q: Push a messy signal through this gate and a clean 1 comes out. Where does the mess go?
frame.at.dig.gate.note: Each gate restores its signal to a clear 0 or 1, so noise does not pile up from one gate to the next.
frame.at.vn.gate.q: Three copies of this gate, and a vote. When is a crowd of unreliable parts more reliable than one good one?
frame.at.vn.gate.note: A vote among three copies outvotes one fault; von Neumann showed in 1956 that reliable machines can be built from unreliable parts.
frame.at.physics.switch.q: Hot silicon leaks, and leaking makes more heat. Fight it with a lower voltage, or put the physics to work?
frame.at.physics.switch.note: Leakage through switches that are off grows quickly as the silicon warms.
frame.at.dig.phoneboard.q: A heartbeat is a smooth wave, but the chip keeps only numbers. How many numbers a second are enough to still call it the same heartbeat?
frame.at.dig.phoneboard.note: Between the skin and the processor sits a converter: the last place on the board where the signal is still a voltage and not yet a number.
frame.at.dig.ecu.q: A failing bearing makes a real tone; a chip that samples too slowly reports a slower tone that was never there. Where did the made-up wave come from?
frame.at.dig.ecu.note: Sampling slower than twice the highest frequency folds fast tones into false slow ones, so a filter must remove them before the converter sees them.
frame.at.vn.soc.q: Billions of transistors, some of them sure to be weak. How does a phone's chip keep working for years anyway?
frame.at.vn.soc.note: Chips carry spare memory rows and codes that catch errors, and are tested and sorted after making, so a weak part is swapped out or the chip is sold to run a little slower.
frame.at.vn.mcu.q: A car maker wants almost no failed chips in a million. How can a small controller be more reliable than any one of its parts?
frame.at.vn.mcu.note: Safety controllers run two cores in lockstep that compare every result, with memories that correct their own flipped bits, so one fault is caught before it acts.
frame.at.perfect.deposit.q: A film that misses the bottom of one trench in billions leaves a hole. Grow it one layer of atoms at a time, or accept some gaps and design around them?
frame.at.perfect.deposit.note: Atomic layer deposition coats every surface evenly by adding one layer of atoms per step, and pays for it by being far slower than other ways of growing a film.
frame.at.eff.print.q: A brighter light source makes each wafer cheaper to print. Will cheaper printing mean less power spent, or many more chips made?
frame.at.eff.print.note: Almost all the electricity that drives an EUV source is lost before light reaches the wafer, so every gain in the source goes straight into more wafers an hour.
frame.at.physics.implant.q: Heat repairs the crystal and switches the dopants on, and the same heat lets them wander. Fight the spreading, or put it to work?
frame.at.physics.implant.note: A laser can heat the surface for a tiny fraction of a second: long enough to switch dopants on, too short for them to spread far.
frame.at.vn.ship.q: In a fleet of millions of chips, faults rare for one chip happen every day. How can the fleet give right answers when some of its chips do not?
frame.at.vn.ship.note: Large fleets have found chips that quietly return wrong results; operators now test chips while they run and retire the ones that slip.
q.bits.q: If information weighs nothing, why does moving it cost so much? Play it as a kitchen: keep the chef busy.

chal.title: Challenge
chal.fast.goal: Make your chip tick one and a half times as fast, with no signal arriving late.
chal.fast.hint: The clock alone can't do it: the slowest signal needs faster switches. Each newer generation shortens it by only about an eighth.
chal.battery.goal: Make the phone's battery last one and a half times as long, at full speed, still with at least 12 cores.
chal.battery.hint: A smaller chip uses less energy but holds fewer cores. What could fit the cores back in?
chal.cores.goal: Give your chip at least 16 cores, while each good chip costs no more than 1.2 times the starting chip's.
chal.cores.hint: A newer process fits more cores, but its wafers cost more. A bigger chip fits more too, but one flaw throws more of it away. Which way keeps the cost down?
chal.quick.goal: Make a chip that needs 50 layers or fewer, still with at least 12 cores.
chal.quick.hint: Older, larger switches need fewer layers. What else could make room for cores?
chal.months.goal: Get your wafers through the fab in under 60 days, while it runs at least 92% full.
chal.months.hint: Near full, every lap waits longer. Could your chip need fewer laps?
chal.fed.goal: Make your chip get two and a half times the starting chip's work done, with every signal on time.
chal.fed.hint: More cores, or a faster clock, only wait faster if numbers cannot reach them. What else has to change?
